Win bought the bear and carried away a lasting conviction that running a hotel would give shape to his life. He and Mary marry and raise five distinctive children: orderly Frank, forceful Franny, observant John, very small Lilly, and young Egg. The family's large dog, Sorrow, adds to the crowded household. Win eventually converts a former girls' school in Dairy, New Hampshire, into his first Hotel New Hampshire. The children grow up among guests, school athletes, and their father's improvisations, learning that the hotel dream will organize the whole family whether or not it becomes financially sensible.

Life at the first hotel brings the Berrys into contact with the neighboring school and its social hierarchy. Chipper Dove and other football players gang-rape Franny. The assault profoundly affects her, though she resists being treated only as a victim. Junior Jones, a Black athlete and genuine friend, stands apart from the boys who harmed her and remains loyal to the family. The siblings close ranks around Franny, with John especially absorbed by his love for her. Frank, who is gay and often targeted by other boys, develops the practical and theatrical skills he uses to survive. Sorrow dies, but the family cannot quite let the dog go; Frank has the body preserved, and a later attempt to reintroduce it into family life has disastrous consequences for their visiting grandfather. The hotel accumulates grief and memory even as Win continues to imagine a grander future.

Freud writes from Vienna with an invitation for Win to take over another Hotel New Hampshire. Win decides to uproot the family for Europe, treating the invitation as the fulfillment of his original dream. During the journey, the plane carrying Mary and Egg crashes, killing them. The surviving Berrys reach Vienna without the household's stabilizing mother or its youngest child. Their new hotel is dilapidated and occupied less by ordinary guests than by sex workers and a group of political radicals. The aged Freud is losing his sight. John, Franny, Frank, Lilly, and Win try to establish routines inside a building whose residents have their own economies, alliances, and secrets. The move that was meant to renew the family instead begins in bereavement and places them in an unfamiliar political world.

In Vienna the family befriends Susie, an American who works in a bear costume and becomes particularly close to Franny. Susie recognizes the continuing effects of Franny's rape and helps her reclaim a sense of physical safety. The radicals, including Ernst and Miss Miscarriage, are preparing a bombing and draw the hotel into their plans. The Berrys discover enough of the plot to resist rather than remain passive hosts. The confrontation turns violent. The intended attack is disrupted, but an explosion kills Freud and blinds Win. Once again the family survives by acting collectively, and once again the cost of Win's hotel dream is borne by people he loves. With the Vienna project ended, the surviving Berrys prepare to return to the United States. Franny, Frank, John, Lilly, and Susie must now find adult roles while caring for a father who can no longer see the condition of the world around him.

Back in America, the siblings convert traits formed in the hotels into careers. Franny becomes a successful actress and Frank proves an effective manager. Lilly writes a celebrated first novel shaped by her experience of being very small, but later struggles to repeat its success and remains distressed by the physical growth that has eluded her. John and Franny continue to carry an incestuous attraction that has shadowed their closeness since adolescence. Rather than build a life around it, they eventually have a single sexual encounter that strips the fantasy of its power and lets them separate as adult partners. Franny's connection with Junior Jones endures, while John's deepest companionship increasingly lies with Susie. Win, now blind, still imagines another functioning hotel, and the family considers how to preserve the hope inside that dream without repeating its earlier forms.

Lilly's despair ends in suicide when she jumps from an open window, adding another death to the family history and giving painful force to the Berrys' repeated warning about enduring moments of hopelessness. Franny establishes an adult life with Junior Jones; Frank continues to guide her career. John and Susie take responsibility for the family's final hotel project. At the old Maine resort where Win first met Mary and conceived his ambition, they create the third Hotel New Hampshire. It is not sustained by ordinary vacationers. Instead, it becomes a protected place for women recovering from rape and abuse, a purpose shaped by what Franny and Susie have survived. John and Susie allow the blind Win to believe he is still the host of a busy, successful hotel. The arrangement preserves his defining dream while redirecting it toward genuine refuge. The surviving Berrys do not overcome their losses, but they keep living together and turn the family's long habit of sheltering its own into care for others.

characters.description: The consulting detective of Baker Street, at the height of his practice and much in demand. He opens the book by reconstructing the life of an unknown visitor from a walking stick left behind in the hall, chiefly to test whether his companion has learned anything from watching him work. He is scornful of superstition, insistent that a case be treated as a problem in evidence, and secretive about his own plans even with his closest friend. Pressure of other work keeps him in London while the case unfolds in Devon, so much of the investigation is conducted at a distance through written reports.
characters.name: Sherlock Holmes

characters.description: A doctor and former army surgeon who shares rooms with Sherlock Holmes and writes up his cases. Practical, brave and conscientious, he is sensitive about being patronised for his slower reasoning. When Holmes cannot leave London he is sent to Devon as the detective's eyes and ears, charged with guarding a client and reporting everything he sees, and he narrates the greater part of the book through his letters and diary.
characters.name: John H. Watson

characters.description: A country doctor practising on Dartmoor, tall, thin and stooping, with a passion for comparative anatomy and the shapes of skulls, and a spaniel that follows him everywhere. He gave up a hospital career to marry and settle in the country. Medical attendant and personal friend to the late Sir Charles Baskerville, he brings Holmes both a family manuscript from the previous century and the facts of a recent death he is not satisfied with.
characters.name: Dr. James Mortimer

characters.description: The late owner of Baskerville Hall, a man who had made a large fortune in South Africa and returned to restore the family estate and spend his money on the district. Nervous, generous and in poor health, he had come to half believe the old family legend and would not walk on the moor after dark. He was found dead at the far end of the yew alley of his own grounds one night, with no mark of violence on him.
characters.name: Sir Charles Baskerville

characters.description: An ancestor of the family in the time of the Great Rebellion, described in a manuscript preserved at the Hall: a violent and dissolute squire who carried off a farmer's daughter and hunted her across the moor when she escaped, and whose own death that night is the origin of the legend of a spectral hound pursuing the Baskervilles.
characters.name: Hugo Baskerville

characters.description: The heir to the Baskerville estate, a nephew of Sir Charles, small, alert and weathered from years of farming in Canada. Newly arrived in England to take up his inheritance, he is level-headed and stubborn, refuses to be frightened away from his own property, and is inclined to treat the family legend as nonsense even after strange things begin happening to him in his London hotel.
characters.name: Sir Henry Baskerville

characters.description: The driver of the cab that carried a bearded stranger who followed Sir Henry through London. Traced by Holmes through the official register, he gives a straightforward account of his fare and repeats, with some enjoyment, the name the passenger gave him.
characters.name: John Clayton

characters.description: The butler at Baskerville Hall, a tall, black-bearded, formal man whose family has served the Baskervilles for generations. He and his wife were the only people in the house when Sir Charles died, and he was left a substantial legacy in the will. He behaves oddly about the household at night and is plainly anxious to leave the Hall and set up in business elsewhere.
characters.name: John Barrymore

characters.description: The housekeeper at Baskerville Hall and the butler's wife, a heavy, impassive woman who keeps the house running correctly while showing every sign of private distress. Watson hears her weeping at night more than once, and her husband denies that anything is wrong.
characters.name: Eliza Barrymore

characters.description: A convicted murderer who has escaped from the prison at Princetown and is believed to be hiding somewhere on the moor. Soldiers and warders are searching for him, the district has been warned, and every isolated household is locking its doors, since he is described as a man who would stop at nothing.
characters.name: Selden

characters.description: A naturalist living at Merripit House on the moor, a small, spare, precise man with a butterfly net who left an unsuccessful career as a schoolmaster in the north of England. He knows the moor and its dangerous bogs better than anyone, is friendly and helpful to the new arrivals, and offers to show Watson the country and the neolithic remains scattered over it.
characters.name: Jack Stapleton

characters.description: The dark-haired, striking young woman living at Merripit House and introduced as the naturalist's sister, in appearance and manner entirely unlike him. Mistaking Watson for the new heir at their first meeting, she urgently begs him to leave Devon at once, and then, when her mistake is discovered, retracts the warning and asks him to forget it.
characters.name: Beryl Stapleton

characters.description: An elderly neighbour at Lafter Hall, a litigious man who spends his money bringing lawsuits against his neighbours and the parish over rights of way and similar questions, and who has quarrelled with his own daughter. His other hobby is astronomy, and he keeps a powerful telescope on his roof with which he watches the moor for the escaped convict.
characters.name: Mr. Frankland

characters.description: A young woman living in Coombe Tracey, the daughter of the litigious Mr. Frankland, who married against her father's wishes and was deserted by her husband. Cut off by her family and earning a precarious living by typewriting, she had been helped quietly by Sir Charles Baskerville, and Watson traces her as the writer whose initials appear in a letter burned in Sir Charles's grate on the night he died.
characters.name: Laura Lyons

characters.description: The Scotland Yard inspector Holmes summons from London at the critical stage of the case, brisk, wiry and openly pleased to be working with him. He arrives by train with no idea of what he is being asked to do and follows Holmes onto the moor at night.
characters.name: Lestrade

recaps.ending: Holmes, Watson and Lestrade lie in wait in the fog outside Merripit House while Sir Henry walks home alone across the moor as bait. An enormous hound, its muzzle and coat smeared with phosphorus so that it burns in the dark, is loosed after him; the three men shoot it dead as it pulls him down, and Sir Henry is left shaken and physically ill but alive. In the house they find Beryl Stapleton tied up and gagged, and she confirms that she is Stapleton's wife, not his sister, and that he has kept the hound in an old tin mine in the heart of the Grimpen Mire. Stapleton flees into the mire in the fog to reach the animal; only one of his boots is ever found, on the path into the bog, and he is presumed to have drowned in it. Weeks later, in Baker Street, Holmes lays out the whole account for Watson: Stapleton was a Baskerville himself, the son of Sir Charles's younger brother, who came to Devon under an assumed name to remove the two lives standing between him and the estate, using the family legend as his instrument. His wife had been coerced into helping him and turned against him at the end. Sir Henry, badly shaken in health, is sent abroad on a long voyage with Dr. Mortimer to recover, with the promise that he will come back the man he was before he inherited.
recaps.in_short: Dr. Mortimer brings Sherlock Holmes an old family manuscript about a spectral hound said to hunt the Baskervilles, and the recent death of Sir Charles Baskerville, found dead in the yew alley of his Dartmoor home with the footprints of a gigantic dog nearby. When the heir, Sir Henry, arrives from Canada, he is warned off by an anonymous letter and shadowed in London, so Holmes sends Watson to Devon with him while he stays behind. On the moor Watson meets the neighbours, including the naturalist Stapleton and the woman introduced as his sister, uncovers the Barrymores' secret help to the escaped convict Selden, and traces Laura Lyons, who was lured into asking Sir Charles for a meeting on the night he died. The convict dies wearing Sir Henry's cast-off clothes, mistaken for him. Holmes has in fact been living secretly on the moor and reveals that Stapleton, a concealed Baskerville heir, is behind the deaths and that his supposed sister is his wife. They use Sir Henry as bait; a phosphorus-painted hound attacks him in the fog and is shot, and Stapleton disappears into the great bog while trying to escape.

recaps.text: At Baker Street, Holmes and Watson examine a walking stick left behind by a caller and deduce the career of its owner, who returns to collect it: Dr. James Mortimer, a country doctor from Dartmoor. Mortimer produces an eighteenth-century family manuscript recording how a brutal ancestor, Hugo Baskerville, carried off a farmer's daughter, pursued her across the moor when she fled, and was found dead beside her with an enormous hound standing over him, and how a curse has followed the family since. He then gives the modern facts. Sir Charles Baskerville, who had restored the family fortune with South African money and was full of plans for the district, was found dead at the end of the yew alley of his own grounds. The inquest recorded heart failure, and there was no mark on him, but his face was distorted, his footprints showed that he had run from the house rather than toward it, and Mortimer says privately that he saw the tracks of a gigantic hound on the ground a little distance away, which he told nobody. Holmes dismisses the supernatural but is interested in the human agency behind it. Mortimer's real difficulty is what to do about the new heir, Sir Henry Baskerville, who is arriving from Canada, and whether it is safe to let him live at the Hall.

Sir Henry Baskerville, a small, hardy young man raised in Canada, arrives in London and comes to Baker Street with Mortimer. He has already received a strange thing at his hotel: an anonymous letter of words cut from a newspaper telling him to keep away from the moor if he values his life. Holmes identifies the newspaper and deduces the message was assembled in a hotel by someone anxious to disguise a hand. Two boots also disappear from Sir Henry's room, one old and one new, and the old one is later returned. Sir Henry insists on going to Devon regardless. Leaving the hotel, Holmes and Watson see a bearded man watching him from a cab and give chase without catching it. Holmes traces the cab through the official register and questions the driver, John Clayton, who reports that his fare followed the party, gave orders through the trap, paid well, and told him that his name was Sherlock Holmes. Unable to leave London himself because of other work, Holmes sends Watson to Devon with Sir Henry, with orders to keep close to him and to report every fact without theorising.

Watson, Sir Henry and Mortimer travel down to Devon, passing armed guards on the road: a convicted murderer named Selden has escaped from the prison at Princetown and is loose on the moor. Baskerville Hall proves to be a gloomy old house run by the butler Barrymore and his wife, who ask to leave once the new master has settled in. Watson hears a woman crying in the night and finds that Mrs. Barrymore has been weeping, though her husband denies it, and he learns that Barrymore was left a large legacy by Sir Charles and cannot account fully for his movements. Watson also establishes that a man with a black beard, as the London watcher had, could have been the butler. Walking on the moor, he meets Jack Stapleton, a naturalist from Merripit House who chases butterflies across country that no stranger could cross safely, and who points out the Grimpen Mire, a bog that swallows ponies and men. A long moaning cry sounds over the moor, which the local people say is the hound. Stapleton's sister Beryl, striking and dark, catches Watson alone, takes him for Sir Henry, and urgently tells him to go back to London and never set foot on the moor again; when she learns her mistake she will not explain herself.

Watson sends written reports to Holmes. Sir Henry is increasingly taken with Beryl Stapleton, and when he manages to speak to her alone her brother rushes at them in a fury, then calls the next day to apologise and explain that he cannot bear the thought of losing her, asking only for a delay of three months. Watson also settles the Barrymore question: following the butler at night, he and Sir Henry find him signalling with a candle from a window to a light out on the moor, and force the truth from him. Mrs. Barrymore's brother is Selden, the escaped convict, and the couple have been feeding him and hiding him until he can be got abroad. Sir Henry and Watson go out to take him and fail; while they are on the moor, Watson sees the outline of a tall, thin man standing motionless against the moon on a distant tor, a figure that is neither the convict nor anyone he knows. Barrymore, in return for their silence, reveals that Sir Charles had gone to the gate that night to meet a woman, and that a burnt letter in the study grate had asked him to be there at ten o'clock and was signed with the initials L. L.

Mortimer identifies the initials as Laura Lyons, the daughter of the quarrelsome Mr. Frankland of Lafter Hall, who married against her father's wishes, was deserted, and lives poorly in Coombe Tracey. Watson calls on her and, after some evasion, she admits writing to Sir Charles to ask his help in paying for a divorce and asking him to meet her at the gate at ten. She insists that she never kept the appointment because help reached her from another quarter that night, and she is plainly frightened of naming the person who encouraged her to write. Riding home, Watson is waylaid by Frankland, who is celebrating his latest lawsuits and boasting that his telescope has shown him a boy carrying food out to a hiding place on the moor, which he believes must be the convict's. Watson goes out alone to the neolithic stone huts on the hillside, finds one that has been lived in, with food, a pannikin and a note recording his own movements, and waits for the occupant to return. The man who walks in is Sherlock Holmes, who has been on the moor in secret from the beginning, watching everyone, including Watson.

Holmes explains that he stayed hidden so that his presence would not put his opponent on guard, and that Watson's reports reached him daily. He has established two things Watson did not: that Beryl Stapleton is not the naturalist's sister but his wife, and that Stapleton is the man who prompted Laura Lyons to write to Sir Charles and then kept her from the meeting. As they talk, a scream comes out of the darkness and they find a body at the foot of a crag, dressed in a suit of Sir Henry's tweeds. It is Selden, who had been given the baronet's cast-off clothes by his sister, and who was hunted to death in mistake for him. Stapleton appears out of the dark, plainly expecting a different body, and covers his reaction quickly. At the Hall, Holmes notices a family portrait of Hugo Baskerville and sees Stapleton's face in it, which supplies the motive: Stapleton is a concealed member of the family with a claim on the estate. Holmes lacks legal proof and sets a trap. He and Watson pretend to leave for London, Lestrade is summoned from Scotland Yard, Laura Lyons is told the truth about the man she trusted, and Sir Henry is told to keep his dinner engagement at Merripit House and to walk home alone across the moor.

Holmes, Watson and Lestrade hide in the open near Merripit House while a fog rolls in off the moor and nearly ruins the plan. Sir Henry leaves the house and walks home alone, and an enormous hound is loosed after him, its muzzle and coat painted with phosphorus so that it burns in the darkness. The three men shoot it dead as it brings him down, and Sir Henry escapes with his life but is severely shaken. Searching the house, they find Beryl Stapleton bound and gagged in an upper room, badly used and finally willing to speak: she is Stapleton's wife, forced for years into playing his sister, and she directs them to an old tin mine on an island in the heart of the Grimpen Mire where the hound was kept. Stapleton has fled into the bog in the fog to reach it, and is never seen again; a single boot of Sir Henry's, used to give the dog the scent, lies on the path where it was dropped. Weeks later, in Baker Street, Holmes sets out the full account. Stapleton was the son of Sir Charles's younger brother, born abroad, who had run a school in Yorkshire under another name before coming to Devon as a naturalist to clear away the two lives between himself and the Baskerville fortune, using the family legend and a savage dog bought in London as his weapon. He frightened Sir Charles, who had a weak heart, into a fatal run down the yew alley, and stole Sir Henry's boots in order to set the hound on him. Sir Henry, worn down in body and nerve, sails on a long voyage with Dr. Mortimer to recover.

characters.description: The Cimmerian king of Aquilonia, once a wanderer, thief, mercenary, and pirate before taking the throne. He is an able soldier with fierce personal courage, but his rule rests on conquest rather than hereditary legitimacy, giving exiled rivals an opening to challenge him.
characters.name: Conan

characters.description: A sorcerer of ancient Acheron restored to life by conspirators who want his power used against Conan. He remembers an empire that vanished thousands of years earlier and regards the present kingdoms as diminished successors fit to be ruled by him.
characters.name: Xaltotun

characters.description: A former priest of Mitra whose study of forbidden lore enables Xaltotun's resurrection. He believes the ancient sorcerer can be controlled long enough to place the conspirators' chosen rulers on the thrones of Nemedia and Aquilonia.
characters.name: Orastes

characters.description: A prince of Nemedia and one of the four men behind Xaltotun's return. Ambitious and calculating, he expects the conspiracy to advance him to his brother's throne while the invasion of Aquilonia removes Conan.
characters.name: Tarascus

characters.description: A powerful Nemedian baron and commander who supplies much of the military force behind the conspiracy. He expects conquest and political influence in return for helping overthrow Conan.
characters.name: Amalric

characters.description: An Aquilonian royal claimant descended from the dynasty Conan displaced. He joins the foreign-backed plot as its candidate for Aquilonia's throne, presenting hereditary blood as his justification for replacing the Cimmerian king.
characters.name: Valerius

characters.description: A young woman serving in the Nemedian palace where Conan is held. She risks approaching the captive king and offers practical help despite having little protection against the powerful men who imprisoned him.
characters.name: Zenobia

characters.description: An elderly witch living apart from court and army. She gives the fugitive Conan shelter and uses uncanny means to help him learn what is happening in his occupied kingdom.
characters.name: Zelata

characters.description: An Aquilonian countess imprisoned by Valerius's regime because of her loyalty to Conan. Her danger shows how quickly the usurper is moving against nobles who will not accept the new rule.
characters.name: Albiona

characters.description: A leader among Aquilonia's followers of Asura, a persecuted faith whose members remember that Conan protected them. He understands more than the court nobles do about the supernatural force behind the invasion.
characters.name: Hadrathus

characters.description: The count of Poitain and one of Conan's strongest remaining vassals. He holds the southern province for the absent king and preserves an organized Aquilonian resistance while the capital is under Valerius's control.
characters.name: Trocero of Poitain

characters.description: A wealthy merchant of Messantia whom Conan knew during his earlier life as a sea rover. He welcomes the fugitive with outward respect, but his prosperity and safety give him reasons to fear involvement in a king's dangerous cause.
characters.name: Publio

characters.description: An ancient Stygian princess encountered in the darkness beneath a pyramid. Supernaturally preserved and alluring, she offers Conan companionship and power if he will abandon his urgent search and remain with her.
characters.name: Akivasha

recaps.ending: Conan returns to Aquilonia with the Heart of Ahriman while Trocero and the loyal provinces gather against the occupiers. Hadrathus uses the jewel to break Xaltotun's supernatural advantage, leaving the resurrected sorcerer unable to determine the battle as he did at Valkia. Conan's forces defeat the invaders; Amalric and Valerius are killed, Xaltotun is destroyed, and Tarascus is captured. Conan demands Zenobia as the price of Tarascus's freedom, repaying the palace woman's earlier rescue by raising her rather than forgetting her. With the foreign army broken and the rival claimant dead, Conan regains the Aquilonian throne. He declares that Zenobia will be his queen, turning the personal debt formed in captivity into the final settlement of his restored reign.
recaps.in_short: Nemedian conspirators revive Xaltotun, a sorcerer of ancient Acheron, to overthrow King Conan. Xaltotun's magic defeats Aquilonia's army, and Valerius takes Conan's throne, but a palace woman named Zenobia frees the captured king. Conan learns that the Heart of Ahriman, the jewel used in Xaltotun's resurrection, can also defeat him. After secretly aiding loyalists in occupied Tarantia and rallying Poitain, Conan crosses the sea and resumes his old identity as the corsair Amra. He reaches Stygia, resists the immortal Akivasha, and recovers the Heart amid rival sorcerers and priests. Returning to Aquilonia, he joins his loyal army for a final battle. Hadrathus uses the jewel to neutralize Xaltotun, the invaders and usurper are defeated, and Tarascus is captured. Conan ransoms Tarascus for Zenobia, restores his kingdom, and names the woman who saved him as his queen.

recaps.text: Orastes, Tarascus, Amalric, and Valerius restore the dead Acheronian sorcerer Xaltotun with a magical jewel called the Heart of Ahriman. Their immediate plan is to use his power to defeat Conan, put Tarascus on Nemedia's throne, and make Valerius king of Aquilonia. As the Nemedian army advances, Conan leads the Aquilonian host at Valkia. Xaltotun sends an unnatural darkness and strikes Conan down before the armies fully engage. Believing their king dead, the Aquilonians lose heart and are routed. Conan awakens as a prisoner rather than a corpse, and the conspirators send him under guard to the palace in Nemedia while their forces move to install Valerius in Tarantia.

Conan learns that Xaltotun is not merely serving the men who revived him: the ancient sorcerer intends to restore Acheron's dominion for himself. In the Nemedian palace Conan is confined in a chamber guarded by a monstrous ape. Zenobia, a young palace servant who has watched him from afar, gives him keys and a knife and explains a route of escape. Conan kills the creature, slips out of the palace, and survives the pursuit into the countryside. The witch Zelata shelters him and helps him see the cruelty unfolding in Aquilonia under Valerius. With his kingdom occupied and his enemies assuming him dead or helpless, Conan begins working his way back toward Tarantia in disguise.

Conan enters occupied Tarantia secretly and finds that Valerius is executing or imprisoning nobles who remain loyal to the old king. He rescues Countess Albiona before the regime can kill her and makes contact with Hadrathus and the followers of Asura, who aid him because he once protected their faith. Hadrathus explains that Xaltotun's life and power are bound to the Heart of Ahriman. The jewel disappeared after the resurrection, and recovering it offers a way to overcome magic that armies alone cannot defeat. Conan sends word to the loyal south, then leaves the capital to join Trocero in Poitain and prepare both a military resistance and a search for the Heart.

Poitain still holds for Conan under Count Trocero, but the king refuses to stake everything on battle while Xaltotun can destroy an army with sorcery. Evidence points toward Stygia as the destination of the missing Heart of Ahriman. Conan travels to the Argossean port of Messantia and seeks help from Publio, a merchant who profited from their earlier association. Publio chooses his own security over loyalty and betrays Conan to the authorities. Conan escapes the trap and reaches the sea, where the skills and reputation of his former life become more useful than royal ceremony. Recognized as Amra, the feared corsair of earlier years, he gains black corsair followers and turns south toward Stygia in pursuit of the jewel.

Conan reaches Stygia and follows the Heart's trail through a landscape ruled by priests, tombs, and rival occult powers. Beneath a pyramid he encounters Akivasha, an ancient princess who preserved herself through vampirism. She tries to persuade him to abandon the surface world and remain with her, but he recognizes the danger and continues his search. The Heart has become part of a struggle among Stygian sorcerers who understand both its power and the threat posed by Xaltotun's return. Conan is repeatedly cut off from ordinary allies, yet his refusal to submit to either terror or temptation carries him closer to the jewel.

Amid violence between Stygian factions, Conan secures the Heart of Ahriman and escapes with the one weapon capable of ending Xaltotun's magical control. He makes the long return north while news and messengers bring the loyal forces of Aquilonia together. Trocero's army is ready to challenge the invaders, and Hadrathus can use the recovered jewel for its intended purpose. The conspirators' alliance is also weakening: Xaltotun's ambition extends far beyond the limited restoration they promised one another, and the men who awakened him can no longer assume that they direct him. Conan rejoins his supporters for the decisive campaign, carrying proof that the supernatural advantage which defeated him at Valkia can be reversed.

Conan and Trocero lead the restored Aquilonian resistance against the occupying army. Hadrathus employs the Heart of Ahriman to strip Xaltotun of the decisive power he used at Valkia, and the resurrected sorcerer is destroyed. With magic no longer controlling the field, Conan's soldiers defeat their enemies; Amalric and Valerius die, ending both the foreign command and the rival claim to Aquilonia's crown. Tarascus survives only to become Conan's prisoner. Conan offers to release him on one condition: Zenobia must be brought safely from Nemedia. Tarascus agrees, and the woman who freed Conan arrives at the restored court. Conan regains his throne and publicly chooses Zenobia as his queen, closing the war by honoring the personal courage that made his return possible.

characters.description: The English novelist at the center of the 1941 prologue. Burdened by recurring mental illness, she leaves her Sussex home, writes a farewell to her husband, Leonard, and walks into the river.
characters.name: Virginia Woolf

characters.description: A New York editor spending a June day preparing a party for her longtime friend Richard, who is receiving a major poetry prize. She lives with her partner, Sally, and remains deeply connected to Richard through friendship, memory, and daily care as his health fails.
characters.name: Clarissa Vaughan

characters.description: A gifted poet and novelist living with advanced AIDS in a disordered New York apartment. Clarissa has known him since their youth and organizes both his practical care and the party marking his literary award. He calls her Mrs Dalloway, linking their present to a summer they shared decades earlier.
characters.name: Richard Brown

characters.description: Clarissa's partner of many years, a television producer whose steadiness contrasts with the intensity of Clarissa's bond with Richard. Their shared home and daughter form the settled life to which Clarissa returns while preparing the evening celebration.
characters.name: Sally Lester

characters.description: Virginia's husband, editor, and publisher, living with her in Richmond in 1923. Attentive to her meals and rest because of her earlier breakdowns, he tries to protect her health while respecting her work, even when she resents the restrictions surrounding her.
characters.name: Leonard Woolf

characters.description: A pregnant California homemaker in 1949, married to Dan and mother to young Richie. While trying to make a birthday cake for her husband, she reads Mrs Dalloway and feels the distance between the competent wife and mother she wants to appear and the life she inwardly experiences.
characters.name: Laura Brown

characters.description: Laura and Dan's observant young son. He watches his mother closely as he helps her prepare Dan's birthday cake, responding to changes in her mood even when he cannot understand them.
characters.name: Richard Brown

characters.description: Laura's affectionate husband, a veteran whose return from the war helped create the suburban family life she now inhabits. His birthday gives Laura's day its outward purpose, and his uncomplicated devotion intensifies her fear that she cannot become the wife he believes her to be.
characters.name: Dan Brown

characters.description: Virginia's sister, a painter who arrives from London with her children. Her ease, vitality, and city life attract Virginia, while the visit also exposes the strain between Virginia's need for protection and her longing to escape Richmond's careful routine.
characters.name: Vanessa Bell

characters.description: Laura's confident friend and neighbor, who comes to the Brown house frightened by a medical problem. Laura admires the ease with which Kitty seems to occupy conventional domestic life, though their meeting reveals that Kitty is also vulnerable.
characters.name: Kitty

characters.description: Clarissa and Sally's grown daughter. Intelligent and serious, she is often accompanied by Mary Krull, whose disdain for Clarissa's comfortable domestic world makes Clarissa self-conscious about her choices.
characters.name: Julia Vaughan

characters.description: A former lover of Richard and Clarissa from their youth, when the three imagined lives different from the ones they eventually made. His arrival for Richard's celebration brings the unresolved emotions of that summer into Clarissa's present-day home.
characters.name: Louis Waters

recaps.ending: Richard refuses the party Clarissa has prepared and tells her that he has stayed alive for her. As she watches helplessly, he lets himself fall from his apartment window and dies. The celebration becomes a small gathering after his death. The elderly Laura Brown arrives and is revealed as Richard's mother. She explains that, after surviving the hotel room and giving birth to her second child, she left Dan and the children and made a life in Canada; Dan and the younger child later died, leaving Richard as the family member who carried the abandonment into his art. Clarissa recoils from Laura's choice but also recognizes that Laura chose the life she could endure. Virginia's 1923 day closes with her decision to move back to London and with her fictional plan to let the poet die while Mrs Dalloway lives. In 1941, as the prologue has already shown, Virginia herself dies in the river. Clarissa remains with Sally, Julia, and Laura through the night, grieving Richard while accepting that ordinary hours of pleasure and connection are the life still available to her.
recaps.in_short: Across three time periods, Virginia Woolf begins Mrs Dalloway in 1923, Laura Brown reads it while struggling with marriage and motherhood in 1949, and Clarissa Vaughan seems to live a modern version of it in New York. Clarissa prepares a party for her former lover Richard, a writer dying of AIDS; Virginia weighs creative freedom against the safeguards imposed after her breakdowns; and pregnant Laura briefly plans suicide before returning to her family. Richard jumps to his death before the party. Laura, revealed as his mother, later explains that she abandoned her husband and children after the birth of her second child because leaving was the only way she could remain alive. Virginia resolves that her fictional heroine will survive even though another character dies, while the prologue establishes Virginia's own 1941 suicide. Clarissa ends the day mourning Richard but still joined to Sally, her daughter, and the difficult continuance of daily life.

recaps.text: In 1941 Virginia Woolf leaves farewell notes for Leonard and walks into the River Ouse, ending her life. The narrative then moves among three June days. In present-day New York, editor Clarissa Vaughan buys flowers for a party honoring Richard Brown, her former lover and closest friend, who is gravely ill with AIDS and has won a poetry prize. In Richmond in 1923, Virginia begins shaping Mrs Dalloway while servants and her husband, Leonard, monitor the routines intended to prevent another mental collapse. In suburban Los Angeles in 1949, pregnant Laura Brown reads Woolf's novel in bed before joining her young son Richie to make a birthday cake for her devoted husband, Dan. Each woman approaches an outwardly ordinary day while privately measuring the life she has made against one she might have lived.

Clarissa visits Richard's apartment to make sure he will attend the party. Ill, confused, and hearing voices, he questions whether the prize and celebration have meaning, while Clarissa tries to keep him anchored to the day's plan. Their exchange shows how thoroughly his care structures Clarissa's day and how uncertain he is that he can continue to meet its demands. In Richmond, Leonard's concern over Virginia's breakfast and work exposes the careful routine imposed after her illnesses. Virginia resents the supervision even while recognizing the danger it is meant to contain. Laura and Richie continue trying to produce the right birthday cake for Dan. The imperfect result deepens Laura's feeling that ordinary domestic acts require her to play a role she cannot naturally inhabit.

Clarissa returns home to preparations involving Sally, her daughter Julia, and Julia's forceful friend Mary Krull, whose presence makes Clarissa examine the settled domestic identity she has built. Laura's confident friend Kitty visits before going to the hospital for tests. Laura comforts and unexpectedly kisses her, then returns to the failed birthday cake and her sense that she is performing a part. Virginia's sister Vanessa arrives from London with her children, embodying the energetic city life Virginia misses. The children find a dying bird and make it a small grave, prompting Virginia to contemplate death while continuing to decide the shape of her novel. Across the three days, familiar visits expose needs and fears that each woman has kept beneath an orderly surface.

Louis Waters, who shared Clarissa and Richard's youthful summer, arrives for the celebration and makes Clarissa revisit the kiss with Richard that still represents a lost possibility. Laura leaves Richie with a neighbor and checks into a hotel with a bottle of pills. Reading Mrs Dalloway in the rented room, she imagines taking enough pills to die. She ultimately understands that she could choose death but does not do so that day; she collects Richie and heads home. Virginia remains irritated by Richmond's constraints and frightened by the possible return of symptoms, considering the balance between survival and freedom. The three stories increasingly echo one another through parties, choices about death, and memories of moments that once seemed capable of determining an entire life.

Clarissa goes back to Richard and finds him sitting at an open window. He says that he has remained alive for her and cannot continue. Before she can stop him, he falls from the window and dies. The planned award party is overtaken by his suicide, leaving Clarissa to face the limits of the care around which she has organized her life. Virginia and Leonard agree that they will leave Richmond and return to London. As Virginia works out her novel, she transfers death away from Mrs Dalloway and toward another character, allowing her heroine to continue through the aftermath. In 1949 Laura lies beside Dan after the birthday and thinks about the child she carries and the future expected of her, still aware that the possibility of departure exists.

After Richard's death, the party gives way to a subdued gathering at Clarissa and Sally's home. An elderly Laura Brown arrives and is identified as Richard's mother. She reveals that after the birth of her second child she left her family, moved to Canada, and worked as a librarian. Dan and the younger child later died, while Richard grew up carrying the effects of her departure. Clarissa finds Laura's abandonment terrible but cannot deny that leaving enabled Laura to survive. Virginia's 1923 thread closes on her renewed plan for London and her understanding that the writer, rather than her heroine, will eventually die; the prologue has already completed that fate in 1941. Clarissa stays with Sally, Julia, and Laura, mourning Richard and recognizing that a life is made from the hours one continues to inhabit, including brief moments of pleasure amid loss.

characters.description: A gentle, good-natured teddy bear who lives in the Hundred Acre Wood and describes himself as a Bear of Very Little Brain. Devoted to honey and to his friends, he muddles through the Forest's small adventures with hums, kindly intentions, and an accidental sort of wisdom, and he is closest of all to the boy Christopher Robin.
characters.name: Winnie-the-Pooh

characters.description: A very small and easily frightened animal who is Pooh's dearest friend and constant companion. Timid by nature, Piglet nonetheless keeps trying to be brave for the sake of his friends, and his loyalty and good heart matter more than his size.
characters.name: Piglet

characters.description: An old grey donkey with a gloomy, resigned outlook, who expects little and is rarely surprised to receive it. Beneath the melancholy he is fond of his friends in his own way, and the others go out of their way to look after him, beginning with building him a house.
characters.name: Eeyore

characters.description: A bouncy, exuberant tiger who arrives in the Forest as a newcomer and immediately makes himself at home. Bold, cheerful, and entirely sure of himself, he bounces everywhere and insists on finding out what Tiggers do and do not like to eat, causing friendly commotion wherever he goes.
characters.name: Tigger

characters.description: A busy, self-important animal who prides himself on being clever and organized, with many friends-and-relations and a fondness for schemes and plans. Fussy and managing, he means well even when his busy notions do not go as intended.
characters.name: Rabbit

characters.description: A bird regarded by the others as the wisest resident of the Forest, given to long words and grand talk, though his spelling and his learning are not quite as reliable as he supposes. He lives in a lofty house and is consulted on matters that call for brains.
characters.name: Owl

characters.description: A calm, motherly kangaroo who looks after her small child, Roo, and keeps a sensible, caring household. Her practical warmth makes her a steadying presence among the Forest's animals.
characters.name: Kanga

characters.description: Kanga's tiny, lively child, eager and fearless in the way of the very young. He adores excitement and quickly takes to the bouncing newcomer Tigger as a hero and playmate.
characters.name: Roo

characters.description: The young boy who is friend and gentle authority to all the animals of the Hundred Acre Wood. Kind and reassuring, he sorts out difficulties and joins the adventures, and the Forest and its creatures are, in a sense, the world of his childhood.
characters.name: Christopher Robin

recaps.ending: The final chapter turns from the small comedies of the Forest to a quiet farewell. Christopher Robin is growing older and will soon have to leave the Hundred Acre Wood for school and the wider world, though the animals do not fully understand this. He takes Pooh alone to a peaceful, enchanted spot at the top of the Forest, and there, gently and without quite spelling it out, he tries to say goodbye. He asks Pooh to promise to remember him and never to forget, whatever happens as they both grow up. The book does not undo this parting or pretend it away; instead it lingers on the tenderness of it. It closes with the boy and his bear still together in that enchanted place, the narrator leaving them there so that, however much Christopher Robin must move on, a small boy and his bear will always be playing in that Forest.
recaps.in_short: In a series of gentle episodes in the Hundred Acre Wood, Pooh and Piglet build a house for Eeyore, and a bouncy newcomer, Tigger, joins the Forest and sets about discovering what Tiggers like. The friends share small adventures: Tigger gets stuck up a tree and later must be calmed of his endless bouncing, Rabbit hatches a busy scheme, Pooh invents the stick-dropping game of Poohsticks on a bridge, and Piglet performs a brave deed when things go wrong at Owl's house. When a storm blows Owl's home down, Eeyore proudly finds him a new one, which turns out to be Piglet's house, and Piglet generously gives it up so that Piglet moves in with Pooh. At the last, Christopher Robin, who is growing up and must soon go away to school, takes Pooh to a quiet enchanted place to say goodbye, asking him to remember and never quite to forget, and the two are left there together as that childhood world is gently closed.

recaps.text: In the earlier stories, the toys and animals of the Hundred Acre Wood, chiefly the honey-loving bear Winnie-the-Pooh and his small friend Piglet, along with gloomy Eeyore, busy Rabbit, learned Owl, motherly Kanga and little Roo, shared a string of gentle adventures under the friendly eye of the boy Christopher Robin. This book continues in the same world, following the same friends through new episodes in the Forest.

The book opens in the Hundred Acre Wood, where Pooh and Piglet decide to build a house for Eeyore in a corner of the Forest, giving the place its name of Pooh Corner. A lively newcomer arrives: Tigger, a bouncy tiger who turns up at Pooh's door and quickly becomes part of Forest life. Much fuss follows as the friends try to work out what Tiggers like to eat, since Tigger is very sure of himself but not at all sure about food, and one attempt leads to a small expedition involving Kanga and Roo. The early chapters set the cheerful, episodic tone, each a self-contained adventure among the familiar animals.

The gentle adventures continue. Tigger's boldness gets him into a scrape when he and Roo end up stuck high in a tree and must be helped down, proving that Tiggers, whatever they claim, do not climb trees well. Rabbit, always fond of a plan, has a very busy day organizing the others, and there is a passing mystery about what Christopher Robin gets up to in the mornings. Pooh invents a new game, later famous as Poohsticks, in which the friends drop sticks from one side of a bridge and watch to see whose comes out first on the other, a simple pleasure that becomes a favorite pastime by the little river.

The friends turn their attention to Tigger's ceaseless bouncing, which some find too much, and there is a scheme to take him down a peg that does not go quite as planned. Piglet, so often timid, does a very grand and brave thing when trouble strikes at Owl's house during rough weather. When a storm blows Owl's home down entirely, Eeyore sets out importantly to find him a new one and proudly presents a house he has discovered, which turns out to be Piglet's own home. Rather than let Owl be homeless, Piglet generously gives his house up, and the matter is happily settled by Piglet going to live with Pooh.

The final chapter steps away from comedy into a quiet goodbye. It becomes clear that Christopher Robin is growing up and will soon have to leave the Forest for school, though the animals only half understand what is changing. He takes Pooh by himself to a still, enchanted place at the top of the Forest and, gently and a little awkwardly, tries to say farewell. He asks Pooh to remember him and to promise never to forget, however grown-up he may become. The story does not soften the parting away, but ends on its tenderness, leaving the boy and his bear together in that enchanted place so that, whatever comes, a little boy and his bear will always be there, playing.

characters.description: A son of the sea god and hero of the earlier stories, who at this book's opening has fallen with Annabeth into Tartarus, the deepest pit of the underworld, a place no living demigod is meant to survive. Brave, stubborn, and powerful over water, he refuses to be parted from her as the two struggle across a nightmarish landscape toward the underside of the Doors of Death. His loyalty and quick thinking are tested to their limits in a realm where the very air is poison.
characters.name: Percy Jackson

characters.description: A daughter of Athena, a brilliant strategist and architect, who has fallen into Tartarus alongside Percy. Resourceful and clear-headed even in terror, she navigates the pit by wits as much as by strength, determined that the two of them will reach the Doors of Death and rejoin their friends. Her intelligence and resolve carry them through horrors that would break most heroes.
characters.name: Annabeth Chase

characters.description: A son of the sky god and former Roman praetor, steady and dutiful, with command over wind and lightning. With Percy and Annabeth lost below, he helps lead the remaining crew of the Argo II toward the mortal side of the Doors of Death. He continues to weigh his divided loyalty to the Greek and Roman camps as he shoulders more of the burden of the quest.
characters.name: Jason Grace

characters.description: A daughter of Aphrodite with a persuasive charmspeak, braver and more capable with each trial. Loyal to Jason and her friends, she uses her voice and her cool head to steer the crew through danger and to steady frightened allies, growing surer of her own strength on the voyage to Greece.
characters.name: Piper McLean

characters.description: A son of Hephaestus and the inventive builder and pilot of the warship Argo II, able to summon fire and improvise machines from scraps. His jokes still hide a private loneliness at being the odd one out among the couples aboard, a loneliness that shapes his part of the journey as the ship crosses the Mediterranean.
characters.name: Leo Valdez

characters.description: A daughter of Pluto who can draw metals and gems from the earth, gentle and brave, with a growing sensitivity to the mists and magic of the underworld. Close to Frank and to her half-brother Nico, she begins to explore deeper powers over illusion and perception as the crew faces enemies that ordinary strength cannot beat.
characters.name: Hazel Levesque

characters.description: A son of Mars and a skilled archer who can shift into animal forms, loyal and increasingly self-assured, though his life is still bound to a fragile piece of wood he guards. Devoted to Hazel, he keeps proving his courage as the quest grows more perilous, stepping into a larger role among the crew.
characters.name: Frank Zhang

characters.description: A son of the underworld god who commands the dead and travels through shadows, freed after being held captive in the previous book. Solitary, guarded, and drained by his ordeal, he sails with the crew, uniquely able to sense the dead and the Doors of Death, and carrying private burdens he keeps to himself.
characters.name: Nico di Angelo

characters.description: The gruff, club-wielding satyr who chaperones the young demigods aboard the Argo II. Quick to threaten and quicker to fight, he guards his charges fiercely beneath the bluster and keeps a rough order on the ship as the dangers mount.
characters.name: Gleeson Hedge

characters.description: The primordial earth goddess, still stirring toward full wakefulness. Speaking through the ground and through dreams, she drives her giants and monsters against the demigods and schemes to keep the Doors of Death open so her forces cannot be stopped, edging ever closer to the moment she can rise and remake the world.
characters.name: Gaea

recaps.ending: Both journeys converge on the House of Hades in the Greek region of Epirus. In Tartarus, Percy and Annabeth reach the Doors of Death with the help of the kindly Titan Bob and the giant Damasen, who give their lives so the two demigods can pass through, and the couple emerges battered but alive on the mortal side. There the rest of the crew has fought its way to the same place, and together they seal the Doors of Death, cutting off Gaea's endless supply of revived monsters. Along the way the heroes have grown stronger and closer: Hazel has mastered a magic of illusion, Frank has come into his full power, and Leo, briefly cast away on the hidden island of Ogygia, has fallen in love with the immortal Calypso and sworn to return and free her. With the Doors closed and all seven reunited, the crew turns toward Athens, where Gaea intends to wake fully and where the giants plan to make their final stand. To keep the Greek and Roman camps from destroying each other in the meantime, Nico di Angelo, the Roman leader Reyna, and Coach Hedge take on the dangerous task of carrying the Athena Parthenos statue across the world to Camp Half-Blood as a token of peace. The book ends with the two efforts underway: the ship racing to Athens for the reckoning with Gaea, and the statue's bearers setting out to prevent a war between the camps.
recaps.in_short: The story follows two paths. Below, Percy and Annabeth struggle across Tartarus toward the underside of the Doors of Death, surviving on nerve and each other, and are aided by a gentle, memory-clouded Titan named Bob and a lonely giant, Damasen. Above, the crew of the Argo II, Jason, Piper, Leo, Hazel, Frank, Nico, and Coach Hedge, sails to the House of Hades in Greece to close the Doors from the mortal side so their friends can escape and Gaea's forces can be shut out. Along the way each hero grows: Hazel learns to bend the mist and work magic, Frank comes fully into his strength, Leo is stranded on a hidden island and meets and falls for the sorceress Calypso, and Nico wrestles with secrets of his own. The two groups fight through to the Doors at the same moment; with sacrifices from their underworld allies, Percy and Annabeth escape Tartarus and the Doors are sealed. All seven are reunited, but Gaea's rising nears its climax, and Nico, Reyna, and Coach Hedge set out on a separate mission to carry the Athena Parthenos statue home and stop a war between the Greek and Roman camps.

recaps.text: Previously: Seven demigods, Greek and Roman, were prophesied to stop the primordial earth goddess Gaea, who is waking and raising the giants. After the goddess Hera swapped heroes to force the two long-separated camps together, the Greek hero Percy Jackson, son of the sea god, and the Roman newcomers Hazel and Frank joined the sky god's son Jason and the new demigods Piper and Leo. Aboard the flying warship Argo II they sailed for the ancient lands to close the Doors of Death, the passage that lets Gaea's slain monsters return. Reaching Rome, Annabeth, daughter of Athena, recovered a lost statue meant to reconcile the camps, but in the process she and Percy fell together into Tartarus, the abyss beneath the underworld. As this book opens, the couple is trapped below, trying to reach the underside of the Doors, while their friends sail on toward the House of Hades in Greece to close the Doors from the mortal side and bring them home.

characters.description: An unmarried woman of twenty-nine whose beauty and social training give her access to wealthy New York society but no secure place within it. With only a small income and expensive habits, she is expected to make a rich marriage. She understands that bargain clearly yet repeatedly recoils from the men and compromises that might secure her future.
characters.name: Lily Bart

characters.description: A lawyer and occasional writer who is related to the fashionable Trenors but lives modestly outside their constant social round. His friendship with Lily carries an evident attraction. He values personal freedom and sees the artificiality of her world, though he is not free of its judgments.
characters.name: Lawrence Selden

characters.description: A wealthy Jewish businessman seeking acceptance in the old New York circle that privately disdains him. Shrewd and observant, he understands both Lily's financial vulnerability and the social value of being associated with her.
characters.name: Simon Rosedale

characters.description: A rich, shy bachelor whom Lily identifies as a suitable husband. He collects Americana, avoids social risk, and prefers women whose conduct appears conventional and serious.
characters.name: Percy Gryce

characters.description: Lily's wealthy friend and hostess at the country estate Bellomont. Energetic and socially powerful, she takes it for granted that friends will perform favors within her complicated network of invitations and obligations.
characters.name: Judith Trenor

characters.description: Judy Trenor's husband, a wealthy and coarse man who manages money for his acquaintances. Lily turns to him for help when she believes she needs an investment income to keep pace with her friends.
characters.name: Gus Trenor

characters.description: A beautiful, commanding married woman at the center of Lily's fashionable set. Clever and socially secure, she can be charming when Lily is useful to her and cutting when she feels challenged.
characters.name: Bertha Dorset

characters.description: Bertha's wealthy, anxious husband. He is often ill and deeply dependent on his wife despite his suspicions about her conduct.
characters.name: George Dorset

characters.description: Lily's rich, widowed aunt, with whom Lily lives when not visiting friends. Mrs. Peniston gives her niece a home and a limited allowance but dislikes disruption and does not understand the scale of Lily's debts.
characters.name: Mrs. Peniston

characters.description: Selden's cousin, a kind and practical young woman who lives simply and devotes much of her time to charitable work. She admires Lily while also recognizing how different Lily's needs are from her own.
characters.name: Gerty Farish

characters.description: An adaptable society woman who supports herself by advising wealthy acquaintances, arranging parties, and helping newcomers enter fashionable circles. She understands social decline as a practical problem and offers Lily the kind of work available to women of their class.
characters.name: Carry Fisher

characters.description: A charming young man in the Dorsets' circle whose lack of money leaves him vulnerable to the wishes of wealthier friends. His closeness to Bertha becomes a source of tension during the Mediterranean voyage.
characters.name: Ned Silverton

characters.description: The cleaning woman at Selden's apartment building. After finding letters written by Bertha Dorset, she offers to sell them to Lily because she assumes Lily can use them.
characters.name: Mrs. Haffen

characters.description: A working-class woman whom Lily once helped through Gerty's charity. When they meet again much later, Nettie is married, caring for a baby, and eager to credit Lily's small act of kindness with helping her rebuild her life.
characters.name: Nettie Struther

recaps.ending: With her health and prospects failing, Lily receives the small legacy left by Mrs. Peniston. She writes a check to Gus Trenor for the full amount she owes him, leaving herself almost nothing. She visits Selden, tells him that she has tried to preserve the best part of herself through her memory of their bond, and secretly burns Bertha Dorset's letters rather than use them to regain social power. After meeting Nettie Struther and seeing the stable home built by a woman she once helped, Lily returns to her room with a renewed but fragile sense of connection. She takes chloral to sleep and dies from an overdose; the narration leaves uncertain whether she miscalculated or dimly accepted the risk. Selden arrives the next morning intending reconciliation and finds her dead. He discovers the check to Trenor and understands that the debt he had judged as evidence of an affair was financial. At her bedside, he recognizes both their love and the failures of courage and trust that kept them apart.
recaps.in_short: Beautiful but nearly penniless Lily Bart moves through wealthy New York society hoping to marry securely without surrendering her independence. She loses Percy Gryce, accepts money she thinks Gus Trenor has invested for her, and is later threatened when Trenor treats the funds as a personal claim. Though Lily possesses letters that could damage Bertha Dorset, she refuses to use them. Bertha then makes Lily the scapegoat for her own affair during a Mediterranean cruise, destroying Lily's reputation. Disinherited by her aunt and gradually abandoned by fashionable friends, Lily tries paid social work and millinery but lacks the skills and health to sustain herself. Simon Rosedale offers a path back if she uses the letters; again she refuses. A small legacy lets her repay Trenor in full. After a final conversation with Lawrence Selden, whom she loves, Lily burns the letters and later dies from an overdose of sleeping medicine. Selden finds her and finally understands both her innocence and the love they failed to act upon.

recaps.text: Lawrence Selden encounters Lily Bart alone at Grand Central Station and invites her to tea at his apartment. Their easy, intimate conversation reveals both Lily's attraction to him and her practical need to marry a rich man. As she leaves, Simon Rosedale sees her emerging from the building, creating a fact that could be used against her. On the train to Bellomont, Lily cultivates Percy Gryce, a wealthy and conventional bachelor. At the Trenors' country house she appears well placed to secure him, but bridge losses deepen her financial anxiety. She is divided between the safety Gryce represents and the freedom she associates with Selden, who arrives unexpectedly among the guests.

Lily's private walk with Selden makes clear that they understand and desire one another, but neither offers a practical future. Bertha Dorset, protecting her own interests, poisons Percy Gryce against Lily by drawing attention to Lily's gambling and unconventional conduct. Gryce withdraws, and Lily loses the marriage she had nearly arranged. Her debts continue to rise. She asks Gus Trenor to invest her small funds, and he soon gives her checks that she accepts as profits. The money restores her confidence and enables her to remain in fashionable company. Meanwhile Mrs. Haffen offers Lily a packet of Bertha's compromising letters to Selden. Lily buys them to prevent their circulation, then keeps them rather than destroying them.

Lily helps make a fashionable entertainment at the Wellington Brys' house a success, appearing in a staged portrait that intensifies Selden's admiration. She begins to hope he will declare himself. Instead, Gus Trenor lures her to his empty New York house and demands personal repayment for the money he has supplied; Lily realizes there were no legitimate investment profits. She escapes him in terror and seeks refuge with Gerty Farish. Selden, who had been moving toward a proposal, sees Lily leaving Trenor's house late at night and assumes the worst. He leaves for Europe without confronting her. Lily is left with a large moral and financial debt, a damaged reputation, and no clear ally.

Lily joins Bertha and George Dorset on a Mediterranean cruise, serving as a social buffer while Bertha pursues Ned Silverton. When George confronts Lily with his suspicions, Lily refuses to confirm his wife's affair. Bertha protects herself by publicly excluding Lily and implying that Lily has behaved improperly with George. The accusation leaves Lily stranded abroad and spreads through New York society. Carry Fisher helps her return, but her standing has collapsed. Mrs. Peniston then dies and, offended by reports of Lily's conduct, leaves most of her estate to another relative. Lily receives only ten thousand dollars, payable after a year—roughly enough to settle her obligation to Trenor but not enough to restore her life.

Lily's former friends keep their distance, and she moves into the less secure circle of Mrs. Hatch, a wealthy young divorcée whom Carry Fisher is helping into society. Selden warns Lily that the household's ambiguous arrangements will further damage her name, and she leaves despite having few alternatives. Simon Rosedale proposes a strategy: Lily should use Bertha's letters to force Bertha to readmit her, after which marriage to Rosedale would become socially valuable to him. Lily refuses to blackmail Bertha. George Dorset, still desperate for evidence against his wife, also seeks Lily's help, but she will not use what she knows. Her refusal preserves her private standards while closing the most direct routes back to wealth and status.

Lily attempts to support herself at a fashionable millinery workroom, but years of ornamental training have not prepared her for regular skilled labor. She becomes exhausted, makes mistakes, and loses the job. She withdraws from Gerty and Carry as shame and sleeping medicine narrow her daily life. Rosedale sees that her social value has fallen too far for his earlier marriage plan, though he offers practical help and remains impressed by her refusal to use the letters. Lily learns that her aunt's legacy will finally be paid. With the money available, she can at last repay Gus Trenor, but doing so will consume nearly all she has.

Lily visits Selden and speaks indirectly of the bond between them, wanting to leave him with the knowledge that it preserved something in her despite her decline. She places Bertha's letters in his fire, surrendering her final instrument of social revenge. Afterward she meets Nettie Struther, a woman she once helped through Gerty's charity, and spends time in Nettie's modest home with her husband and baby. The visit shows Lily a form of family stability outside the world that rejected her. Back in her room, Lily writes Gus Trenor a check that repays every dollar and takes chloral to sleep. She dies from an overdose. Selden arrives the next morning ready to acknowledge his love, finds her dead, and discovers the check. It proves that Trenor's claim on her was a debt rather than an affair. At Lily's bedside, Selden understands that love existed between them but that distrust and hesitation prevented them from saving it.

characters.description: A powerful Puritan landowner who secured Matthew Maule's property during the witchcraft persecutions and built the seven-gabled mansion on it. His sudden death at the house's first great gathering begins the pattern of guilt and misfortune associated with the Pyncheon family.
characters.name: Colonel Pyncheon

characters.description: The original owner of the ground on which the Pyncheon house is built. He resists Colonel Pyncheon's claim, is condemned as a wizard, and at his execution leaves words that later generations remember as a curse on the Pyncheons.
characters.name: Matthew Maule

characters.description: The elderly, impoverished mistress of the House of the Seven Gables. Proud of her family's former position yet devoted to her absent brother, she overcomes her fear of public notice to open a small shop in one of the gables.
characters.name: Hepzibah Pyncheon

characters.description: A young daguerreotypist who rents part of the Pyncheon house. Independent and skeptical of inherited rank, he becomes one of Hepzibah's first customers and views the old family's habits with an outsider's alertness.
characters.name: Holgrave

characters.description: A neighborhood boy and eager customer at Hepzibah's newly opened shop. His appetite for gingerbread helps turn her alarming experiment in trade into an ordinary part of local life.
characters.name: Ned Higgins

characters.description: An elderly handyman and familiar figure in the neighborhood. Poor but sociable, he offers Hepzibah practical sympathy and treats the prospect of eventually living at the poorhouse with cheerful equanimity.
characters.name: Uncle Venner

characters.description: Hepzibah's young country cousin, who comes to stay at the old house. Capable, warm, and untroubled by aristocratic pride, she quickly improves both the cent shop and the spirits of the people living behind it.
characters.name: Phoebe Pyncheon

characters.description: Hepzibah's beloved brother, returned to the family home after decades in prison. He is frail, frightened, and poorly suited to ordinary demands, but remains exceptionally responsive to music, flowers, and Phoebe's gentle company.
characters.name: Clifford Pyncheon

characters.description: A wealthy cousin of Hepzibah and Clifford, publicly admired for dignity and benevolence. His resemblance to the ancestral Colonel and Clifford's terror of him make his offers of family assistance appear far less reassuring inside the old house.
characters.name: Jaffrey Pyncheon

characters.description: A beautiful Pyncheon ancestor whose fate is described in the story Holgrave reads to Phoebe. Raised in privilege and confident of her place, she becomes the unwilling means through which her father tries to recover a lost family claim.
characters.name: Alice Pyncheon

characters.description: Alice's father, a merchant determined to establish the Pyncheon family's title to valuable eastern land. He asks a descendant of the Maules to use his unusual powers in the hope that Alice can reveal where the missing evidence lies.
characters.name: Gervayse Pyncheon

characters.description: A young carpenter descended from the condemned Matthew Maule and bearing the same name. Summoned by Gervayse Pyncheon, he agrees to mesmerize Alice but uses the bond to assert the Maule family's power over the people who displaced them.
characters.name: Matthew Maule

recaps.ending: Judge Pyncheon dies in the parlor from the same inherited condition that killed his ancestor, rather than by Clifford's hand. The Judge had allowed Clifford to be blamed for the earlier death of their uncle after concealing his own presence at the scene, and his pressure on Clifford was an attempt to recover information about supposed Pyncheon wealth. Hepzibah and Clifford return after their frightened train journey, and the Judge's death eventually frees them from his power. His only son is already dead, so his property passes to Clifford, Hepzibah, and Phoebe. Holgrave tells Phoebe that he descends from the Maules; their decision to marry unites the two families without continuing the old contest over the house. The heirs move to the Judge's country estate and invite Uncle Venner to live with them. They leave the seven-gabled mansion behind, exchanging the family's decayed monument and inherited grievances for a shared future elsewhere.
recaps.in_short: Impoverished Hepzibah Pyncheon opens a cent shop in her family's decaying mansion and welcomes home her fragile brother Clifford after decades of wrongful imprisonment. Their country cousin Phoebe revives the household and grows close to Holgrave, a radical daguerreotypist lodging in a gable. Wealthy Judge Jaffrey Pyncheon tries to force Clifford to disclose a supposed family secret, repeating the greed of the ancestral Colonel, who took Matthew Maule's land during the witchcraft persecutions. The Judge dies suddenly while waiting in the parlor, causing Hepzibah and Clifford to flee in fear, but his death proves natural. He had helped direct suspicion toward Clifford when their uncle died years before. Holgrave reveals that he is a Maule descendant, and his love for Phoebe ends rather than renews the family feud. The surviving Pyncheons inherit the Judge's estate and leave the old house for his country home, taking Uncle Venner with them.

recaps.text: The House of the Seven Gables occupies land once held by Matthew Maule, who was executed as a wizard after refusing to yield his claim to Colonel Pyncheon. The Colonel builds his mansion there but dies suddenly at its opening celebration, and the family remembers Maule's last words whenever later Pyncheons meet similar misfortune. Generations afterward, the family has lost most of its wealth. Elderly Hepzibah Pyncheon lives almost alone in the deteriorating house and reluctantly opens a cent shop to support herself. The work conflicts with her inherited pride and her fearsome expression discourages customers, but a neighborhood boy and the young lodger Holgrave make the shop's first day a modest success.

Uncle Venner, an elderly neighborhood handyman, offers Hepzibah sympathy as she adjusts to trade. Her young cousin Phoebe arrives from the country and quickly makes herself useful, handling customers and bringing order and warmth to the dark rooms. Hepzibah has also been preparing for the return of her brother Clifford after roughly thirty years in prison. He arrives physically aged and emotionally fragile, taking comfort in Phoebe's voice and in beautiful objects while shrinking from harsh faces and practical demands. When wealthy Judge Jaffrey Pyncheon visits, Hepzibah blocks his entrance. Although he presents himself as a generous relative, Clifford's fear and the Judge's strong resemblance to the ancestral Colonel make his interest in the household threatening.

Phoebe becomes Clifford's steady companion, leading him into the garden and helping him enjoy a limited domestic peace with Hepzibah, Holgrave, and Uncle Venner. The old man nevertheless remains separated from ordinary life. Watching the street through the arched window briefly excites a wish to join the passing crowd, but he cannot sustain it. Holgrave, who opposes the authority claimed through wealth and ancestry, studies Judge Pyncheon through his daguerreotype and believes the image exposes a hardness hidden by the man's respectable public expression. Phoebe is drawn to Holgrave but remains cautious of the cool, experimental way he sometimes regards the Pyncheons and their long history.

Holgrave reads Phoebe a family story about Alice Pyncheon. Her father Gervayse sought the missing proof of the Pyncheons' claim to a large eastern territory and called on a young carpenter named Matthew Maule, grandson of the executed man. Maule mesmerized Alice but, rather than merely helping locate the document, retained influence over her and repeatedly humbled her until she died. While reading, Holgrave realizes that Phoebe too has become receptive to his influence and deliberately releases her, refusing to repeat the old abuse. Phoebe then leaves for a short visit home. Without her, Clifford and Hepzibah sink back into the house's gloom. Judge Pyncheon returns, determined to question Clifford about the source of wealth he believes the family can still recover, and threatens further confinement if Hepzibah does not cooperate.

Hepzibah goes upstairs but cannot find Clifford. Back in the parlor, Clifford shows her Judge Pyncheon sitting dead in his chair. Convinced that Clifford will again be accused, the brother and sister flee and board a train. The movement briefly gives Clifford a sense of freedom, but they soon turn back toward home. The Judge has died from a hereditary disorder like the one that killed Colonel Pyncheon. His missed appointments and plans continue without him while the corpse remains alone in the house. Phoebe returns and finds Holgrave watching over the property. He explains the death and declares his love for her, establishing a future no longer governed by the mansion's past.

The history behind Clifford's imprisonment becomes clear. When the Pyncheons' wealthy uncle died suddenly, the younger Jaffrey concealed evidence of his own presence and let suspicion fall on Clifford. Judge Pyncheon's death now removes the power that sustained that injustice. His son has already died abroad, leaving Clifford, Hepzibah, and Phoebe to inherit his property. Holgrave reveals that he belongs to the Maule line, but his engagement to Phoebe joins the families and rejects the inherited struggle between them. The new heirs leave the House of the Seven Gables for the Judge's country estate and bring Uncle Venner with them. The old mansion remains standing, but its surviving residents no longer organize their lives around its claims, secrets, and remembered curse.

characters.description: A former nobleman serving ten years of hard labor in a Siberian prison after being convicted of killing his wife. His notes record the routines, punishments, cruelties, and relationships of prison life from the perspective of a newcomer isolated by class and temperament.
characters.name: Alexander Petrovich Goryanchikov

characters.description: The unnamed acquaintance who introduces Alexander after his release from hard labor and later obtains the dead man's papers. His frame narrative presents the prison memoir as a document discovered among those papers.
characters.name: The Editor

characters.description: A former military officer imprisoned among the common convicts. Exact, rule-bound, and unusually concerned with order and propriety, he helps Alexander understand the prison's arrangements during his first days.
characters.name: Akim Akimovich

characters.description: The prison commandant, notorious among the convicts for violent rages, arbitrary discipline, and an unnerving watchfulness. His authority makes every encounter with him dangerous.
characters.name: The Major
